# Chapter 02 | From statistics to full-stack ownership

[← Previous](01_THE_ENGINEER.md) · [Table of contents](../OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md) · [Next →](03_SYSTEMS_IN_THE_WILD.md)

## My technical origin

I studied **Statistics and Data Science** at the University of Pretoria, graduating with a BCom in 2023. That education still shapes how I approach software engineering. I start by asking whether the data supports the statement somebody wants to make. A model can be mathematically correct while the source events, sample, joins or time window are wrong.

My professional path moved outward from analytical questions.

## Timeline of practice

| Period | Environment | What I learned |
|---|---|---|
| **2023** | University projects and early analytics exposure | Statistics, predictive reasoning, reproducibility and the importance of data definition |
| **2023–2024** | Broadcasting and enterprise reporting | Operational SQL, media/service KPIs, automation, reporting under deadlines |
| **2024–2025** | Consulting across banking, capital markets, FMCG and media | Power BI, DAX, stakeholder definitions, security-aware analytics across organisations and markets |
| **2025–early 2026** | Agriculture, social impact and independent experimentation | ERP/NAV mappings, data capture workflows, business adoption, cross-system reasoning |
| **January–August 2026** | Remote Australian manufacturing delivery | SQL Server, Fabric, Power Automate, logistics and workforce models, production/scheduling reporting |
| **August 2026 onward** | Data/BI and full-stack platform responsibility | TypeScript backends, APIs, PostgreSQL, tenant access, admin workflows, security, cloud and testing |

Dates are broad career context, not an assertion that every engagement was continuous or full-time. The [case-study record](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md) provides engagement-level descriptions.

## Three turning points

### 1. The grain of the data mattered more than the chart

In industrial and commercial reporting, there are many plausible tables to join. A schedule row, a dispatch, a production batch and an invoice are not necessarily the same business event. A naive join can multiply facts. I learned to define the grain, choose stable keys, check cardinality and reconcile back to the source before trusting a DAX measure.

**What changed:** I stopped thinking of Power BI as the place where incorrect upstream semantics should be patched.

### 2. Automation changed the value of the work

Producing the same manual report every week teaches an obvious lesson: the repeatable task should be engineered. Automated SQL extracts, dataflows, scheduled reports and controlled transformations reduced human hand-offs and made failures easier to investigate.

My historical CV reports reductions of **up to 70% in manual reporting effort** in some engagements. That is a reported historical result, not a public benchmark reproduced by this repository.

**What changed:** I began measuring usefulness in work removed from the process, not only charts added to a page.

### 3. The data product became a software product

Platform work taught me that a metric may need an API, a permissions model, a transaction, a workflow, an audit log and deployment gates. The user's experience and the correctness of the database are not separate disciplines.

**What changed:** I took a stronger interest in TypeScript, React, PostgreSQL, authentication, background jobs, cloud infrastructure and release engineering.

## Cross-industry pattern recognition

The industries may look unrelated, but I keep finding the same failure modes:

- **Financial services:** date-aware measures, restricted information and auditability.
- **Manufacturing:** grain, operational latency, workforce/scheduler alignment and source-system drift.
- **FMCG and research:** large data volumes, survey joins, data-quality assumptions and commercial interpretation.
- **Media:** linking sentiment, contact, service-level and customer experience signals.
- **Agriculture:** bridging ERP/NAV semantics and decision-ready reporting.
- **Education and social impact:** privacy, consent, human interpretation and long-lived records.

The tools vary; the underlying engineering questions persist.

## How I now explain my career

I have been an analyst, BI developer, data engineer, application builder and the person debugging the pipeline when everyone is waiting for the dashboard. That range is not proof that I have expert-level experience in every technology. It means I have learned to take responsibility for **the whole path from problem to useful outcome**.

For the detailed engagement record, see [Client case studies](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md). For what I am building independently, continue to the next chapter.

# Chapter 03 | Systems in the wild

[← Previous](02_THE_CAREER.md) · [Contents](../OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md) · [Next →](04_DATA_ENGINEERING.md)

A career is easier to understand through the systems and constraints behind it than through a list of logos. This chapter is a guided tour of what I have worked on, why it was difficult and what kind of evidence a reviewer can inspect.

## 01. Enterprise banking analytics across four markets

**Status:** Historical professional delivery. **Practice:** Power BI, DAX, Power Query, access-aware reporting.

I worked on commercial and retail reporting spanning **South Africa, Namibia, Botswana and Zambia**, with a documented portfolio of **18 banking dashboards**. Regional reporting changes the problem: access controls, product definitions, local market contexts and time comparisons have to remain intelligible as the audience expands.

**Engineering focus:** improve model relationships, simplify expensive measure logic, challenge over-broad access and remove repeated manual transformations. My CV reports a **40% improvement in dashboard load time** on relevant optimisation work.

**What I learned:** a fast report showing inconsistent numbers is not a successful optimisation. Establish the semantic contract, then measure performance.

**Evidence:** [Professional case-study record](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md#3-fnb--iqbusiness-consulting-commercialretail-analytics). Client code and data remain proprietary.

## 02. Commercial research at survey scale

**Status:** Historical professional delivery. **Practice:** large survey datasets, Power Query, DAX, marketing analytics.

A documented FMCG engagement involved cleaning, modelling and visualising **more than 270 million survey records** for commercial insights. Large volumes turn small modelling mistakes into expensive mistakes, especially when joining outlets, campaigns, brands and survey responses at mismatched grains.

**Engineering focus:** careful transformations, model efficiency, metric definitions and meaningful breakdowns for business owners.

**What I learned:** scale alone is not the achievement. The real product is a trusted commercial measure that users can explain.

**Evidence:** [Research and FMCG case studies](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md#5-diageo-africa--iqbusiness-large-scale-brand-analytics). The record is historical; these are not public raw datasets.

## 03. Manufacturing and logistics in Australia

**Status:** Historical delivery. **Practice:** SQL Server/T-SQL, Power BI, DAX, Power Automate, Fabric workflows.

I supported remote Australian manufacturing operations, where reports linked production, dispatch, stock, employee scheduling and operational timing. A scheduler model documented in my CV included **15 temporary SQL tables, 35 DAX measures, 11 relationships and reporting across eight states**.

**Engineering focus:** reason about event grain, repair dataflow failures, support accurate production-versus-hours reporting, and automate recurring delivery. Complex SQL became useful only after the business event and join path were defined.

**What I learned:** the database schema and the real world are different representations. Delivery engineers must understand both.

**Evidence:** [Manufacturing case study](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md#1-bitberry--bestbar--australia-data-platform-manufacturing-and-delivery-analytics). Industrial source systems are not reproduced in this public profile.

## 04. The Fixer: from reporting to governed applications

**Status:** Public implementation with active security, CDC and cloud work; **not** an approved all-features production cutover.  
**Repository:** [NewChanges](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges).

The Fixer explores governed imports and synchronisation from SQL views, APIs and files into employer, partner and administrative reporting. It crosses product boundaries: **TypeScript/Fastify APIs, PostgreSQL/Prisma, a React modernisation track, reporting, authentication and operational controls**.

A current design question is how to connect source updates with dashboard freshness. The simulation work includes a MySQL row-binlog experiment, but the existing ten-feed reporting source still requires an ingestion-specific CDC adapter and dedicated validation. Polling a nullable timestamp is not the same as capturing every change.

**What I learned:** reporting freshness is a contract between source, transformation and consumer, not a UI refresh button.

**Evidence:** [Repository](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges) · [Active CDC integration issue](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/issues/241) · [Security audit issue](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/issues/232).

## 05. CABO Learning Hub: education as a long-lived system

**Status:** Public product under development, with pilot and proposed integrations; **not** a government deployment.  
**Repository:** [Training-and-Development-Hub](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Training-and-Development-Hub).

The product goal is bigger than course delivery: connect learning materials, assessments, teachers, guardians, institutional roles, historical progress and future interventions. I have explored source-grounded written exams and AI-assisted partial-credit marking, with teacher oversight needed for consequential decisions.

Longitudinal educational records create engineering difficulties that ordinary demo apps avoid: learner transfers, role changes, guardian consent, assessment provenance, country jurisdiction and controlled retention.

**What I learned:** a learner is not a row that belongs forever to one school. Data governance must travel with the person and the purpose.

**Evidence:** [Repo status and documented limits](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Training-and-Development-Hub) · [Admissions and transfer epic](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Training-and-Development-Hub/issues/97) · [Year-end progression review issue](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Training-and-Development-Hub/issues/163).

## 06. CABO Financial Intelligence: the transaction is the truth

**Status:** Staging/prototype, not statutory accounting or auditing certification.  
**Repository:** [Accounting, Audit and Analytics Software](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Accounting-Audit-And-Analytics-Software).

This independent product explores a **double-entry ledger, exact-decimal values, immutable journals, atomic invoice settlements, bank CSV reconciliation, period locking and audit review**. Reporting consumes the controlled transactional state rather than altering it.

A vital separation: generated financial explanations may help a reader understand a report, but they must not silently create, amend or approve journal entries.

**What I learned:** in financial workflows, an atomic transaction and a documented reversal matter more than a dashboard animation.

**Evidence:** [Repository and capability matrix](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Accounting-Audit-And-Analytics-Software) · [Mission dossier](../OMNIMASTER_MISSION_DOSSIERS.md#mission-06--cabo-financial-intelligence).

## 07. CABO Human Capital: decisions need accountable humans

**Status:** Public prototype and synthetic development.  
**Repository:** [HR-Software](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/HR-Software).

Recruitment and workforce software deals with incomplete evidence, privacy, fairness and people whose opportunities may depend on the output. I have explored role-scoped candidate workflows, review history, evidence provenance and AI-assisted recommendations.

**What I learned:** a score without an explanation is not better decision-making. Humans need to remain accountable for meaningful hiring and development decisions.

**Evidence:** [HR software repository](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/HR-Software) · [Mission dossier](../OMNIMASTER_MISSION_DOSSIERS.md#mission-05--cabo-human-capital).

## 08. Social impact and smaller operational products

**Status:** Historical volunteer work plus public prototypes.

In social-impact reporting I worked with capture processes and dashboards for service outcomes. Independent work in artist management, commerce and bookings has explored how enquiries, identities, transactions and notifications form usable business workflows.

**What I learned:** even a small application needs an identifiable business event, an authoritative state change and an accessible path for the user.

**Evidence:** [Volunteer case study](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md#9-jozi-my-jozi--social-impact-analysis) · [Artist Management Hub](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Artist-Management-Hub) · [CABO Solutions website](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/CABOSOLUTIONS).

## Reading the range correctly

These examples are not eight claims of production certification. Some are historical professional delivery, some are inspectable public implementations, and others are unfinished product experiments. What connects them is the engineering approach: **start with the real operational problem, make definitions explicit, enforce correct transitions, and prove the system's behavior**.

[Complete project inventory](../PROJECT_PORTFOLIO.md) · [Detailed mission dossiers](../OMNIMASTER_MISSION_DOSSIERS.md)

# Chapter 04 | Data engineering as a discipline

[← Previous](03_SYSTEMS_IN_THE_WILD.md) · [Contents](../OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md) · [Next →](05_ANALYTICS_ENGINEERING.md)

My starting principle is simple: **data cannot become reliable by changing its colour in a dashboard**. Reliability begins with source events and continues through extraction, transformation, storage, serving and recovery.

## A pipeline is a sequence of contracts

~~~mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Operational SQL / APIs / files"] --> B["Source identity, grain and access"]
    B --> C["Ingestion & checkpoint"]
    C --> D["Quality, lineage & modelling"]
    D --> E["Curated data / semantic model"]
    E --> F["APIs, BI, operational decisions"]
    F --> G["Reconciliation, monitoring, rollback"]
~~~

Every arrow is a place data can be lost, duplicated, misclassified or delayed.

## 1. Define the grain before writing the join

Imagine an operational system with one order, three deliveries and five quality observations. Joining all three at the raw record level can multiply the order amount fifteen times. That is not a DAX error; it is a relational grain mismatch.

**My review sequence:**

1. State each table's business event and unique key.
2. Identify one-to-many relationships and expected cardinality.
3. Reconcile counts and amounts before and after joins.
4. Determine whether to aggregate early, create bridge tables or model separate facts.
5. Add tests for unexpected duplicate keys and late-arriving events.

This is the same thinking I have used in manufacturing, banking and research analytics.

## 2. Separate business time from modification time

A payment may have occurred in June, been corrected in July and been ingested in August. These are different facts: **event time**, **source modification time** and **pipeline processing time**. Historical reports may need any of the three.

An updated timestamp that is nullable, rounded to one second or never advanced by manual updates cannot by itself guarantee lossless incremental loads.

**Design questions:** Can multiple updates share a watermark? Can a record be deleted physically? What happens to a correction for a closed period? Is the source query repeatable? Can the pipeline resume after a partial write?

## 3. Choose polling, CDC or batch on purpose

| Strategy | Useful when | Failure to anticipate |
|---|---|---|
| **Scheduled batch** | Daily reports and stable extraction windows | Missed windows, late files and inconsistent snapshots |
| **Watermark polling** | Source exposes reliable version/update keys | Same-timestamp writes, nullable values and invisible deletes |
| **Row-binlog CDC** | Changes must be captured continuously or near-continuously | Binlog retention, transaction ordering, checkpoints and read privileges |
| **Event publishing** | The source application can emit durable domain events | Producer/consumer contracts, duplicates, retries, poison messages |

The Fixer's MySQL source work has been exploring these boundaries. Its existing reporting views and synthetic binlog laboratory are **not yet the same production pipeline**. See [CDC integration work](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/issues/241).

## 4. Bronze, Silver, Gold is a contract, not a naming scheme

- **Bronze:** preserve source identity, payload, ingestion metadata and replay evidence.
- **Silver:** produce validated, typed, deduplicated and business-consistent records.
- **Gold:** curate consumer-level measures and aggregates at a documented grain.

In Microsoft Fabric or Databricks these layers can be implemented using lakehouse and Delta-style patterns where appropriate. In my public [CDC Replay Lab](../../projects/cdc-replay-lab/), a small SQLite program illustrates the semantics without pretending to be a managed distributed lakehouse.

## 5. Let each validation own a real risk

I do not want every component to reimplement a slightly different definition of an email address, effective date or identifier. Validation should be deliberate:

- **At the source boundary:** check structure, required keys, contract type and authorisation.
- **In the database:** enforce relationships, uniqueness and transactional consistency.
- **At the business layer:** apply domain policy with explicit error handling and audit.
- **At the consumer:** explain freshness, completeness and interpretation.

The [Data Quality Contracts Lab](../../projects/data-quality-contracts/) shows a deliberately small contract with readable failures instead of silent repairs.

## 6. Design the failure path before release

I expect a pipeline to encounter duplicate input, a malformed record, transient network errors, unavailable secrets, unexpected schema changes and backfills. My preferred evidence includes:

| Failure | Recovery property |
|---|---|
| Same event delivered twice | Idempotent handling or detected duplicate |
| Worker restarts mid-batch | Transactional checkpoint with no lost committed work |
| Source timestamp is ambiguous | Explicit warning or alternate change mechanism |
| Destination write partially fails | Rollback, retry and clear dead-letter handling |
| A user loses access | Server-side scope enforcement and revocation tests |
| Historic source records change | Recompute impacted aggregates rather than full arbitrary rewrite |

## A reproducible design exercise

Open [CDC Replay Lab](../../projects/cdc-replay-lab/) and trace one account through create, update and delete operations. Repeat the events. Check that the current projection stays correct and the event log retains the deletion. Then inspect what the toy example lacks: source transaction capture, a durable source checkpoint, cross-entity ordering and multi-writer consistency.

**The distinction between a demonstration and a production pipeline is part of the lesson.**

Further reading: [System design playbook](../OMNIMASTER_SYSTEM_DESIGN.md) · [Source contract and mission history](../OMNIMASTER_MISSION_DOSSIERS.md)

# Chapter 05 | BI, semantic models and decision systems

[← Previous](04_DATA_ENGINEERING.md) · [Contents](../OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md) · [Next →](06_PRODUCTS_AND_AI.md)

BI is often treated as a presentation layer. My experience suggests it is closer to **a governed interpretation layer** between operational activity and decisions.

## The anatomy of a trustworthy metric

Consider “active customer rate.” A meaningful implementation must specify:

- **Population:** which users are included?
- **Observation window:** today, rolling 30 days, a financial month or programme-to-date?
- **Activity definition:** logins, transactions, settled balances or something else?
- **Grain:** person, account, transaction or organisation?
- **Access boundary:** which employers, markets or teams may see the result?
- **History:** how do corrections, deleted records or changing memberships affect earlier periods?

Without these definitions, two teams can both report a plausible percentage and both be wrong for the decision at hand.

## Where I developed this discipline

Banking reporting across four African markets, 270M+ survey records in a commercial research engagement, Australian production and scheduling reporting, and ERP/NAV-derived agricultural analytics exposed me to different kinds of measure ambiguity.

In each case, correctness required conversations with business owners **and** careful source analysis. I have written DAX, Power Query transformations and SQL, but the most valuable step is often getting agreement on what a metric *means*.

## My semantic-model review checklist

| Layer | What I inspect | Typical symptom |
|---|---|---|
| **Source** | Stable keys, nulls, event date, reconciliation totals | Data differs from operational system |
| **Relationships** | Star-schema grain, direction, ambiguous paths, many-to-many joins | Totals change when unrelated filters are applied |
| **Measures** | Filter context, denominators, time intelligence, blank handling | Percentage exceeds expected range or historical figures drift |
| **Security** | Row-level access, market/employer separation, export paths | A user can inspect another organisation's measure |
| **Performance** | Query plans, cardinality, repeated transformations, visuals | Slow page loads and excessive model scans |
| **Delivery** | Refresh status, source latency, missing periods, fallbacks | “Live” dashboard shows stale data |

## Practical performance reasoning

A slow dashboard invites many unhelpful fixes: adding more compute, reducing visuals arbitrarily or caching incorrect results. I start by isolating where time is spent.

1. Profile source query and row counts.
2. Check filter predicates, indexes and aggregation grain.
3. Review model relationships and DAX query patterns.
4. Determine whether work should happen once in SQL/ELT rather than repeatedly per visual.
5. Re-measure with comparable filters and data.
6. Verify the resulting business numbers did not change.

My previous CV reports a **40% dashboard-load improvement** in an optimisation engagement and reductions in manual report work of up to **70%** in some workflows. Those numbers describe professional experience; this repository does not include client performance logs.

A small related exercise: [SQL Query Plans Lab](../../projects/sql-query-plans/). It compares a full scan against a composite-index range search on fictional data. SQLite is a teaching tool here, not a benchmark for Power BI, Fabric or SQL Server.

## Modern data platforms without cargo-cult architecture

I have worked with SQL Server, Power BI and Microsoft Fabric-related analytics, and developed skills in PySpark/Databricks patterns. My evaluation of any new stack asks: Do we need distributed processing? Who owns the transformation? What is the cost of moving the data? Is there a stable semantic layer? What happens during source correction?

A sophisticated lakehouse architecture is useful when its scale, history, governance or interoperability justify it. It is not automatically superior to a clear and well-indexed SQL query.

## How I explain technical decisions to business users

I translate “the join changes row multiplicity” into “the same delivery has been counted more than once.” I translate “watermark collision” into “two legitimate updates may arrive with the same timestamp, so the report could miss one.” I translate “role-based access” into “an employer must only see people and metrics they are allowed to see.”

**A good analytic product gives decision-makers confidence about its assumptions, not merely colourful certainty.**

# Chapter 06 | Software products and responsible AI

[← Previous](05_ANALYTICS_ENGINEERING.md) · [Contents](../OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md) · [Next →](07_SECURITY_AND_DELIVERY.md)

I became more interested in full-stack development as I discovered how often the useful outcome was **an action, not a chart**. A user may need to complete onboarding, verify an enrolment, correct a record, approve a financial entry or receive a trustworthy explanation.

## The system underneath the screen

~~~mermaid
flowchart TD
    UI["React / native client"] --> API["Authenticated API boundary"]
    API --> POLICY["Roles, validation and business rules"]
    POLICY --> DB["Transactional database"]
    POLICY --> EVENTS["Jobs, audit events, notifications"]
    POLICY --> AIB["Optional AI service boundary"]
    AIB --> EVAL["Schema validation, source evidence, fallback"]
    EVAL --> REVIEW["Human review when consequential"]
    EVENTS --> OBS["Observability and recovery"]
~~~

This is an architectural pattern, not a statement that every public project implements every component.

## Three product examples

### A. Data integration and reporting: The Fixer

The Fixer crosses application and analytical boundaries. Users configure permitted sources, inspect ingestion, review reporting, interact with dashboards and administer permissions. That creates a requirement to protect both **data-plane** access and **control-plane** changes.

**Engineering questions:** Who may change a source URL? Can a source connection reach a private network address? How are invalid files rejected? What does an audit event prove? Can an administrator bypass step-up authentication through a different route?

**Public evidence:** [NewChanges](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges). Active release/security PRs remain separate from any public claims of deployment readiness.

### B. Learning and assessment: CABO Learning Hub

The Learning Hub explores source-grounded exams, written responses, marking feedback and long-term education journeys. It combines document ingestion, user-scoped records, educators, guardians and institutional permissions.

**Engineering questions:** Can a model invent a question unsupported by the document? Does marking exceed the rubric's maximum score? Can staff inspect another learner's record? Who can correct an AI-suggested grade? How do school transfers affect data ownership?

**Public evidence:** [Training-and-Development-Hub](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Training-and-Development-Hub). High-stakes academic decisions must remain human-governed.

### C. Accounting and audit: CABO Financial Intelligence

The product explores a double-entry ledger, reconciliations, immutable audit context and optional AI-powered *explanation*. Transactions and controls must be deterministic. A generated sentence should never be treated as a write instruction.

**Public evidence:** [Accounting, Audit and Analytics Software](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Accounting-Audit-And-Analytics-Software). Staging status and functional limits are documented in the repository.

## The difference between an AI integration and an AI feature

Calling a language model is easy. Delivering a responsible feature needs more:

| Design dimension | What I ask |
|---|---|
| **Task** | What useful action does this support, and what remains deterministic? |
| **Input** | Is the source authorised, bounded, relevant and appropriately redacted? |
| **Output contract** | Does the response conform to a validated schema and business rules? |
| **Grounding** | Can the response point back to approved documents or facts? |
| **Human control** | Can someone review, reject, override and contest the result? |
| **Failure behaviour** | Is the feature useful when an AI provider is unavailable? |
| **Operating cost** | Is model selection appropriate for latency, quota and budget? |
| **Safety** | Can prompts, attachments or outputs leak information or bypass roles? |

In Learning Hub experiments, I have explored task-aware routing across Groq and Hugging Face with fallback. A previous isolated provider test demonstrated Groq operation and degradation fallback, while Hugging Face's live response was blocked by an HTTP 402 billing/credit condition at the time. **A fallback demonstration is not proof that both providers work in production.**

[AI routing workstream](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Training-and-Development-Hub/pull/95)

## A deliberately small evaluator

My [Offline AI Output Evaluation Lab](../../projects/ai-output-evaluation/) does not call a model. It validates synthetic *extractive* answers for known source IDs, exact quotations, expected shape and explicit human-review requirements. It deliberately rejects unsupported freeform additions.

It is useful as a teaching example precisely because its limits are visible. A matching quote does not prove the source is true or safe, a caller-supplied confidence score is not calibration, and a simple email-pattern check is not privacy protection.

## The cost of a careless automated decision

Children's learning, employment and financial decisions affect real lives. I favour:

- Documented purpose and lawful access before processing.
- Access-scoped retrieval and data minimisation.
- Quality evaluation with synthetic and approved representative cases.
- A meaningful path for a person to challenge or correct the result.
- Auditable decisions, cautious retention and carefully bounded provider calls.
- Explicit release blockers when legal, privacy or security review is outstanding.

For the Botswana education direction, jurisdiction and data-transfer requirements require verified legal and hosting assessments **before any live learner-data rollout**. A product roadmap is not legal approval.

[System-design playbook](../OMNIMASTER_SYSTEM_DESIGN.md) · [Learning Hub repository](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Training-and-Development-Hub)

# Chapter 07 | Security, testing and the path to release

[← Previous](06_PRODUCTS_AND_AI.md) · [Contents](../OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md) · [Next →](08_REPRODUCE_THE_WORK.md)

My engineering work has increasingly involved release ownership, where the difficult question is not “does it work once?” but **“what happens when it fails, when someone misuses it, or when the environment changes?”**

## Security is a collection of trust boundaries

~~~mermaid
flowchart LR
    U["User / device"] --> S["Session and MFA"]
    S --> A["Authorisation policy"]
    A --> API["API and domain rules"]
    API --> DB["Least-privilege data access"]
    API --> OUT["Approved external services"]
    DB --> AUDIT["Audit and restore controls"]
    OUT --> AUDIT
~~~

The diagram is a review checklist, not a certification of a particular deployment.

## My practical review lenses

| Boundary | Example failure | Evidence I want |
|---|---|---|
| **Authentication** | Password-only account reaches privileged routes | Real HTTP negative tests, session expiry and re-authentication |
| **MFA / recovery** | TOTP replay succeeds or recovery bypasses policy | Replay, lockout, key handling, passkey and recovery tests |
| **Authorisation** | User swaps an ID and reads another tenant | Cross-tenant negative tests and least-privileged DB role |
| **Source ingestion** | URL validation passes, second DNS lookup connects elsewhere | Pinned transport or enforceable egress controls, SSRF tests |
| **Database operations** | Partial transaction commits | Atomicity, retry, rollback and concurrent-update tests |
| **Output safety** | CSV cell becomes spreadsheet formula | Export encoding tests and safe quoting |
| **Delivery** | A staging “green” is treated as a production sign-off | Exact-commit CI, migration and recovery evidence |
| **Secrets** | Keys leak to logs or frontend | Secret scanning, least privilege and rotation procedures |

## The Fixer security work as a real-world example

The Fixer has active work around mandatory administrator TOTP and WebAuthn, enrolment, session revocation, auditability, source URL safety and security scanning.

The public [MFA draft PR](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/pull/219) and [security remediation PR](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/pull/233) demonstrate a difference I care about: code can be implemented and reviewed without the feature being cleared for release. These changes have required Docker integration checks, browser tests, real roles, deployment-safe keys and migration validation. **An unmerged draft is not a shipped production control.**

One security audit used a local AI scanner. Thousands of generated observations were not thousands of demonstrated vulnerabilities. Model suggestions need source-level evidence, an exploit mechanism, deterministic tests and a disposition. The corresponding [audit triage issue](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/issues/232) remains an engineering task, not a green security badge.

## How I want tests organised

1. **Static and unit checks:** formatting, types, pure functions, boundary cases.
2. **Database tests:** disposable DB, real transactions, constraints, isolation and rollback.
3. **API tests:** authenticated HTTP requests with both happy-path and denial-path checks.
4. **Browser/mobile tests:** genuine user workflows, narrow screens and accessible states.
5. **Security checks:** known risky inputs, secret/dependency/SAST checks and authorisation abuse cases.
6. **Release rehearsal:** migration, backup restore, rollback and exact environment configuration.

A passing unit suite is valuable. It does not establish that a database migration will succeed, a credential will be configured, or a browser flow will remain usable.

## CI is evidence, not decoration

In my GitHub profile, the [Engineering Labs workflow](../../.github/workflows/engineering-labs-ci.yml) runs standard-library tests for four synthetic projects when relevant files change. That verifies local educational examples. It does **not** substitute for the self-hosted Docker and external-service tests required by the larger platforms.

For product releases, I favour:

- Pinning tests to an exact commit.
- Running disposable databases and explicit negative cases.
- Blocking merges on required gates when possible.
- Keeping production secrets out of test artifacts.
- Separating “not run”, “failed”, “passed”, and “not applicable”.
- Treating cost and service availability as operational constraints.
- Never switching live data stores without final sync, writer fencing, rollback and approval.

## Where the learning came from

I have debugged source failures, failed CI, incompatible database assumptions, auth and MFA design questions, cloud migration trade-offs and dependency upgrade risks. The recurring lesson is that the cheapest time to uncover a failure is **before someone relies on the release**.

I want to be the engineer who can explain why a deployment is ready, and also explain why it is not.

# Chapter 08 | Reproduce the work

[← Previous](07_SECURITY_AND_DELIVERY.md) · [Contents](../OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md) · [Next →](09_LEADERSHIP_AND_NEXT.md)

A recruiter can read an architecture paragraph in sixty seconds. An engineer should also be able to inspect code and run a small example. These four labs are designed for exactly that: **synthetic inputs, no cloud credentials, no customer data and explicit tests**.

## Quick-start

Requires Python 3.12 or a compatible modern Python environment.

~~~bash
git clone https://github.com/CayelaemJ/CayelaemJ.git
cd CayelaemJ

cd projects/cdc-replay-lab
python -m unittest discover -v
cd ../data-quality-contracts
python -m unittest discover -v
cd ../sql-query-plans
python -m unittest discover -v
cd ../ai-output-evaluation
python -m unittest discover -v
~~~

The [GitHub Actions lab workflow](../../.github/workflows/engineering-labs-ci.yml) also runs all four suites on relevant PRs. Inspect the latest run before claiming that a new change passed.

## Lab 1. CDC Replay

**Path:** [projects/cdc-replay-lab](../../projects/cdc-replay-lab/)  
**Concepts:** immutable event ID log, latest-state projection, idempotency, order-by-source-sequence, tombstones and atomic failure.

**Exercise:** apply an account UPSERT, update it, DELETE it, then replay the same event IDs. The Gold aggregate should not double-count, and the Bronze record should show what happened.

**Production boundary:** no live binlog reader, distributed checkpointing, encryption, service identity or multi-writer transaction guarantee.

## Lab 2. Data Quality Contracts

**Path:** [projects/data-quality-contracts](../../projects/data-quality-contracts/)  
**Concepts:** required schema, duplicate keys, decimals, timezone-aware timestamps and freshness.

**Exercise:** pass a valid row, then a duplicate ID, a future timestamp and a NaN amount. Inspect the structured violations rather than silently modifying the input.

**Production boundary:** these are illustrative policies, not the actual validation rules of a bank or regulated system.

## Lab 3. SQL Query Plans

**Path:** [projects/sql-query-plans](../../projects/sql-query-plans/)  
**Concepts:** query-plan inspection, composite indexes, date-range filtering, sargability and unchanged aggregation results.

**Exercise:** compare a query plan before and after adding an index. Then wrap the indexed date in a function and examine what part of the index SQLite can use.

**Production boundary:** the in-memory SQLite result is not a cloud warehouse, Fabric or SQL Server benchmark.

## Lab 4. Offline AI Output Evaluation

**Path:** [projects/ai-output-evaluation](../../projects/ai-output-evaluation/)  
**Concepts:** evidence IDs, exact source quotes, structured outputs, invalid confidence, unsupported answer additions and human-review flags.

**Exercise:** invent a citation, alter an evidence quote, append an unsupported conclusion or introduce sensitive text. Observe how the evaluation refuses the response.

**Production boundary:** no external LLM is called. Quote matching is not semantic truth, model calibration, privacy certification or prompt-injection resistance.

## What the tests prove

| Lab | Local unit tests added and exercised | What is still outside scope |
|---|---:|---|
| CDC Replay | 5 | Actual source CDC and distributed recovery |
| Data Quality | 5 | Enterprise-specific policies and large datasets |
| SQL Plans | 6 | Production DB performance |
| AI Evaluation | 8 | Empirical LLM quality and complete safety |
| **Total** | **24** | The tests establish toy-example behaviour, not whole-product readiness |

The four suites have a passing GitHub Actions verification on the preceding portfolio CI work, and the handbook documentation must be checked separately. See the workflow for current evidence.

## Suggested review questions

- Which event or record is authoritative, and how is it identified?
- What invariant would fail if the same input arrived twice?
- Which outcome cannot be inferred from a unit-test success?
- If I changed the business grain or row-level access scope, what would have to change in the model?
- What happens when an AI provider fails or the input contains untrusted instructions?

That is the kind of conversation I prefer: working through assumptions and evidence, not counting badges.

# Chapter 09 | How I work and where I am going

[← Previous](08_REPRODUCE_THE_WORK.md) · [Contents](../OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md) · [Next →](10_GLOSSARY_AND_EVIDENCE.md)

My ambition is to grow toward **solution architecture, principal engineering and technology leadership**, ultimately earning the scope and judgment required of a CTO. I am not presenting a future title as a current one. I am interested in the responsibility: making better technical decisions, developing reliable teams and owning the consequences.

## The kind of engineer I am

I have often worked in places where the reporting problem is a database problem, the database problem is a business-definition problem, and the business-definition problem cannot be solved without a conversation with the people who operate the process.

That shapes my delivery style:

**I investigate.** Before replacing technology, I inspect source contracts, actual errors, query plans, runtime limits and constraints.

**I implement.** SQL, APIs, UI, background jobs, tests and deployment are connected work. I aim to understand where the change will have an effect.

**I communicate.** Non-technical users need to know whether the numbers are correct and when they will change, not the complete stack trace.

**I document.** If a feature is a draft, an infrastructure cutover is staged or an AI provider is unavailable, the status should be visible.

**I protect trust.** I prefer clear refusals, tenant-aware permissions, reversible migrations and honest release status over a convenient but unsafe shortcut.

## Working with business, product and engineering

| Situation | How I approach it |
|---|---|
| Conflicting KPI definitions | Ask for one agreed business event, population, time window and owner; write tests and examples |
| Stakeholder wants a faster report | Reproduce and measure the bottleneck, preserve correctness, communicate the change |
| Product request spans multiple layers | Draw the flow, define contracts, identify owner of state transitions, split verifiable work |
| Security finding appears | Validate its mechanism with source and a test; distinguish a scanner observation from a vulnerability |
| Deadline threatens release quality | State what is verified, what is blocked, and what reversible scope can safely ship |
| AI-generated output influences people | Use bounded assistance, provenance, human review and a correction path |

The skill I want to sharpen most is **technical judgment under real constraints**: balancing reliability, cost, time, team capability, law, security and customer value.

## Roles where my background fits

| Role family | Why it fits | The growth edge I am developing |
|---|---|---|
| **Data Engineer / Data Platform Engineer** | SQL, ETL/ELT, source contracts, modelling, performance and pipeline ownership | Broader streaming, distributed orchestration and large-scale operations |
| **Analytics Engineer / BI Engineer** | Power BI, DAX, semantic models, access-aware reporting and business definition | Enterprise semantic governance and deeper platform observability |
| **Full-Stack / Platform Engineer** | React, TypeScript, API/backend, databases, authentication and release testing | Larger system boundaries, resilience and team-scale design |
| **Applied AI Engineer** | Embedding guarded AI calls in workflows, source evidence, evaluation and fallback | Formal evaluations, monitoring, data governance and production ML operations |
| **Solution Architect pathway** | Can connect business goals to data, applications and security requirements | Documented architecture leadership, cross-team decisions and mentoring |

This is a map of relevant work and developing strengths, not a claim to have served in all of these titles.

## What I would like a technical interview to explore

I would rather discuss one system deeply than recite definitions.

A meaningful conversation could examine a real-world source-change problem, why a dashboard went stale, how to avoid duplicate financial transactions, how to protect learners across institutions, or how a model-assisted grading workflow could fail safely.

A strong discussion might start with:

> How would you trace a discrepancy from a visual all the way back to the source event, without hiding it behind another validation layer?

That question captures much of my experience.

## The direction of the next chapter of my career

I want to lead toward systems that are **useful, scalable where necessary, cost-aware, secure and explainable to their users**. I'm developing independent technology products partly because shipping complete experiences exposes gaps that a narrowly scoped reporting task may never reveal.

I am also learning to distinguish between *building the feature* and *building the organisation that can safely maintain it*. Effective technical leadership needs architecture, documentation, hiring and mentorship, reliable delivery processes and the confidence to say no to unsafe shortcuts.

I do not want to become detached from the code. I want to keep enough depth to understand the trade-off behind the decision.

- [Public code and engineering labs](https://github.com/CayelaemJ)
- [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/cayelaem-jantjies-000b45144/)

# Chapter 10 | Glossary, references and claim register

[← Previous](09_LEADERSHIP_AND_NEXT.md) · [Contents](../OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md) · [Return to cover](../../README.md)

This last chapter is here because technical language should make work understandable, and public evidence should not quietly turn aspiration into achievement.

## A working glossary

| Term | What I mean when I use it |
|---|---|
| **Business grain** | The one real-world event or entity represented by one row of a fact or source table |
| **Data contract** | Explicit source/output schema, keys, semantic meaning, ownership and permitted changes |
| **ETL / ELT** | Extract-transform-load or extract-load-transform; the correct choice depends on where transformations belong |
| **Watermark** | Position or value used to identify new/changed data; its precision and reliability determine what can be missed |
| **CDC** | Change data capture, typically recording actual changes rather than repeatedly rereading a full source |
| **Idempotency** | Repeating the same operation has no unintended additional effect |
| **Tombstone** | Evidence of a deletion maintained for consumers rather than silently removing historical change context |
| **Bronze / Silver / Gold** | Raw or auditable intake, curated validated records, and consumer-ready aggregates or views |
| **Semantic model** | Business-aware analytical relationships, dimensions, measures, security and time interpretation |
| **Star schema** | Facts at a defined grain connected to shared descriptive dimensions |
| **DAX** | Formula language for analytical measures and calculations in Power BI and related Microsoft tools |
| **RLS** | Row-level security, restricting which data a database or semantic-model user can access |
| **RBAC** | Role-based access control; identity alone is not permission |
| **MFA / TOTP / WebAuthn** | Multi-factor authentication, time-based one-time codes, and passkey/security-key standards |
| **SSRF** | Server-side request forgery, including tricks that push a server into connecting to unauthorised endpoints |
| **SAST** | Static application security testing; findings require analysis, not blind acceptance |
| **Sargable query** | A query shaped to let the database efficiently use indexes on searchable predicates |
| **Human-in-the-loop** | A meaningful human control over consequential system or model output, not a decorative checkbox |
| **Exact-commit CI** | Tests and checks tied to the specific source commit being considered for merge or release |
| **Deployment gate** | A requirement that must be satisfied before enabling a candidate in the intended environment |

## Claim register: what you can verify here

| Claim or theme | Nature of evidence | Primary reference |
|---|---|---|
| BCom in Statistics and Data Science (2023) | Education history from CV, not independently validated by GitHub | [Career case studies](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md), [profile timeline](../../README.md) |
| 3+ years across analytics and engineering | Professional history as documented by CV and engagement summaries | [Career record](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md) |
| 270M+ survey records | **CV-reported historical scope**, not a public dataset benchmark | [FMCG case study](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md#5-diageo-africa--iqbusiness-large-scale-brand-analytics) |
| 40% dashboard load-time improvement | **CV-reported historical outcome**, not rerun here | [Banking case study](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md#3-fnb--iqbusiness-consulting-commercialretail-analytics) |
| Up to 70% manual reporting reduction | **CV-reported historical outcome**, dependent on engagement | [Professional cases](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md) |
| Banking analytics across four markets | Historical work scope | [Banking case](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md#3-fnb--iqbusiness-consulting-commercialretail-analytics) |
| The Fixer implementation | Public code with active issues/PRs; no blanket production readiness claim | [NewChanges](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges) |
| Learning Hub education/AI implementation | Public code, pilots and planned work clearly distinguished | [Training-and-Development-Hub](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Training-and-Development-Hub) |
| Financial and HR products | Public prototype/staging work and explicit limits | [Financial Intelligence](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Accounting-Audit-And-Analytics-Software), [Human Capital](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/HR-Software) |
| Four educational engineering labs | Runnable synthetic source, local tests and GitHub Actions | [Project index](../../projects/README.md), [CI workflow](../../.github/workflows/engineering-labs-ci.yml) |
| CTO or technology leadership | **Future career direction**, not current position | [Chapter 09](09_LEADERSHIP_AND_NEXT.md) |

## How to verify a project responsibly

1. **Start with the README:** identify what the author claims is implemented versus planned.
2. **Look at source and tests:** a file or PR exists, but check what actually executes.
3. **Check CI on the relevant commit:** historical green status does not certify a new head.
4. **Check release status:** staging, pilot, private experiment and production are different environments.
5. **Check privacy boundaries:** absence of client source code is often appropriate, not evidence the engagement never occurred.
6. **Ask about limitations:** I want a reviewer to challenge architectural and evidence assumptions.

## Other long-form references

- [Client case studies](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md): roles, sectors and engagement-level technical history.
- [Project atlas](../PROJECT_PORTFOLIO.md): catalogue and stage of visible independent products.
- [Technical skills and evidence](../TECHNICAL_SKILLS.md): honest skills matrix.
- [Engineering mission dossiers](../OMNIMASTER_MISSION_DOSSIERS.md): deeper system context.
- [System design playbook](../OMNIMASTER_SYSTEM_DESIGN.md): practices and trade-offs.
- [Engineering field notes](../ENGINEERING_FIELD_NOTES.md): current workstreams and lessons.
- [Runnable labs](../../projects/README.md): reviewable Python, SQL and evaluation examples.

## Epilogue

I want my GitHub to be useful to three kinds of readers: somebody who wants to understand me as an engineer, somebody who wants to inspect how I think, and somebody who wants to verify code rather than trust a headline.

That is why this handbook contains **career history, real project constraints, executable examples and limitations side by side**.

**One mind. Every layer. No pretending a roadmap is a release.**

# Field Guide 01 | Annotated architecture atlas

[← Volume II contents](../OMNIMASTER_FIELD_GUIDE.md) · [Next: Debugging casebook →](02_DEBUGGING_CASEBOOK.md) · [Main handbook](../OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md)

Architecture only becomes useful when it reveals who owns the facts, where trust changes and how a system handles failure. These are **reference architectures inspired by my work**, not exact deployment diagrams, infrastructure inventories or promises that every component is live.

## Map A. From operational updates to trustworthy analytics

**Context:** my current MySQL and PostgreSQL reporting experiments, historical enterprise BI work and the [CDC Replay Lab](../../projects/cdc-replay-lab/).

~~~mermaid
flowchart LR
    SRC["Operational system / MySQL"] --> CAP{"Capture contract"}
    CAP -->|"Reliable timestamp / batch"| POL["Incremental polling"]
    CAP -->|"Row changes available"| BIN["Binlog / CDC reader"]
    POL --> RAW["Auditable ingestion"]
    BIN --> RAW
    RAW --> VAL["Typed & keyed projections"]
    VAL --> SEM["Source-aware business model"]
    SEM --> BI["Dashboard / API"]
    RAW --> CP["Checkpoint & reconciliation"]
    CP -->|"Replay / repair"| VAL
~~~

**What matters at each boundary**

| Boundary | Question I ask | A useful test |
|---|---|---|
| Operational source → capture | Are deletes, corrections and same-timestamp updates observable? | Apply multiple writes with one timestamp; compare extracted changes |
| Capture → raw store | Is a source event durable before the checkpoint advances? | Crash between event write and checkpoint |
| Raw → curated state | What is the correct grain? Are duplicate messages harmless? | Replay the same event ID; verify unchanged totals |
| Curated state → metrics | Are changed and deleted accounts reflected without double counting? | Compare dashboard aggregates with controlled source truth |
| Metrics → user | What latency is promised, and what counts as “fresh”? | Measure end-to-end lag, not just UI polling interval |

**Trade-off:** binlog CDC can preserve deletion and change order better than naive timestamp polling, but introduces replication privileges, lifecycle, transaction boundaries, retention and operational complexity. It is not an automatically better answer for every low-volume reporting feed.

**Actual delivery boundary:** the [Fixer synthetic binlog work](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/pull/237) is distinct from the ten-feed reporting path; [issue #241](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/issues/241) tracks the needed adapter and proofs. This diagram is the target reasoning model, not a claim of a finished production connection.

## Map B. Semantic modelling that respects the business event

**Context:** banking, FMCG, agriculture and Australian manufacturing analytics. Proprietary source data is deliberately not shown.

~~~mermaid
flowchart TD
    ORD["Orders / dispatch events"] --> G["Declare source grain"]
    EMP["Workers / schedules"] --> G
    SUR["Surveys / campaigns"] --> G
    G --> CT["Cardinality & key tests"]
    CT --> F["Curated fact tables"]
    DIM["Conformed dates, products, locations"] --> MODEL["Governed semantic model"]
    F --> MODEL
    MODEL --> RLS["Market / employer restrictions"]
    RLS --> KPI["Power BI measures & decisions"]
    KPI --> REC["Source reconciliation & performance tests"]
~~~

**Why I draw this:** one delivery can have several processing events; one employee can have multiple shift records; one survey response can join to multiple classifications. Without grain contracts, a dashboard can be *precisely wrong* at impressive speed.

**My working rule:** reconcile a sum or count at each transformation boundary and after security filters. Performance optimisation is valid only if the intended business total survives it.

**Reproducible companion:** [SQL Query Plans Lab](../../projects/sql-query-plans/) illustrates filtering/indexing without claiming to benchmark Power BI or Microsoft Fabric.

## Map C. A full-stack administrative workflow

**Context:** The Fixer and independent full-stack applications.

~~~mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    actor User
    participant UI as Browser or native UI
    participant Auth as Session / MFA
    participant API as Authorised API
    participant DB as Transactional database
    participant Audit as Audit events
    User->>UI: Request sensitive change
    UI->>Auth: Present session and step-up
    Auth-->>UI: Verified proof or denial
    UI->>API: Submit action
    API->>API: Validate role, tenant and input
    alt Authorised
        API->>DB: Atomic write with constraints
        DB-->>API: Commit / failure
        API->>Audit: Record result with actor and scope
        API-->>UI: Correct response
    else Denied
        API->>Audit: Record attempted action as permitted
        API-->>UI: Deny without information disclosure
    end
~~~

**Critical engineering distinction:** front-end access control improves usability but cannot protect an endpoint. Each privileged request needs a server-enforced role and tenant boundary. For MFA, credential enrolment and emergency recovery must not open an unguarded parallel path.

**Actual delivery boundary:** [Fixer admin MFA PR #219](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/pull/219) remains a draft workstream with deployment and negative-test gates, not a completed production security guarantee.

## Map D. Applied AI inside a real product workflow

**Context:** Learning Hub assessment, document grounding and independently developed [AI output checks](../../projects/ai-output-evaluation/).

~~~mermaid
flowchart LR
    USER["Authorised educator / learner"] --> POLICY["Purpose, access and consent"]
    DOC["Approved reference documents"] --> RET["Retrieval & provenance"]
    POLICY --> ROUTER{"Task-specific AI routing"}
    RET --> ROUTER
    ROUTER --> MODEL["Approved model/provider"]
    MODEL --> CHECK["Schema & evidence evaluation"]
    CHECK --> DEC{"Consequential output?"}
    DEC -->|"Yes"| HUMAN["Educator / accountable reviewer"]
    DEC -->|"No"| OUTPUT["Scoped user response"]
    HUMAN --> OUTPUT
    MODEL -. "Unavailable" .-> FALL["Controlled fallback / no-decision state"]
    FALL --> OUTPUT
~~~

A model response is not automatically a grade, an employment decision or a financial posting. A safe process needs a valid input purpose, permitted documents, an output contract, evaluation and a human route for consequential decisions.

**Failure to simulate:** provider 429/402 responses, irrelevant retrieved material, prompt injection in documents, unsupported citations, confidence mismatch, timeout and leakage between learners or tenants.

**Actual delivery boundary:** the [CABO Learning Hub](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Training-and-Development-Hub) has development and pilot work; its [provider routing PR](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Training-and-Development-Hub/pull/95) does not establish fully verified multi-provider production availability.

## Map E. A release that remains reversible

~~~mermaid
flowchart TD
    CODE["Specific source commit"] --> T["Build, unit and integration tests"]
    T --> SEC["Negative security & browser checks"]
    SEC --> MIG["Migration / backup / restore rehearsal"]
    MIG --> READY{"All release gates pass?"}
    READY -->|"No"| HOLD["Hold, fix, retest"]
    READY -->|"Yes"| APPROVAL["Authorised rollout decision"]
    APPROVAL --> RAMP["Staged traffic & observability"]
    RAMP --> HEALTH{"Healthy & correct?"}
    HEALTH -->|"No"| ROLL["Rollback & investigate"]
    HEALTH -->|"Yes"| KEEP["Operate, document, monitor"]
~~~

**Why this matters to me:** I have seen work reach a promising branch or staging environment while remaining unfinished operationally. A migration requires writer fencing, reconciliation, privileged-role review, rollback and evidence tied to the exact change.

The [profile's lab CI](../../.github/workflows/engineering-labs-ci.yml) validates toy examples. It is *not* a substitute for The Fixer's Docker, database, security or actual deployment gates.

## How I use these diagrams in a design review

I ask five questions, in order:

1. Where does the authoritative event originate?
2. Which boundaries can lose or distort information?
3. Who can perform each action, and how is that enforced?
4. What happens when one component fails or retries?
5. Which measurements or tests would tell us the solution actually worked?

The diagram has value only when it gives a colleague something concrete to challenge.
